title: Build a system that turns voice memos into action items
description: A system that turns a voice memo transcript into decisions, action items, and drafted follow-ups for review.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

context.title: Context
context.content: Everything Claude can 'see' in a given session — your messages, files you've shared, instructions, and conversation history. The more relevant context you give Claude, the better its output.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: A decision made out loud on a call, in a meeting, or on a walk rarely becomes a tracked task on its own. This system closes that gap. It takes a recorded voice memo, separates the decisions from the open questions, extracts action items with an owner and deadline, and drafts the follow-up messages for each so you can send them yourself.

Claude can already search a person's own voice-memo transcripts and cite the specific recording where a decision got made, per [Anthropic's Claude Academy personal use cases](https://academy.claude.com/use-cases?department=personal). Turning that same transcript into a tracked list is the step that comes after finding it.
Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) every time you record, a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill), or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that runs on new transcripts automatically.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming what you usually record, where the transcripts come from, who needs to see follow-ups, and how urgency gets flagged.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that turns my voice memos into tracked action items. Ask me questions, one at a time, about what I usually record, where my transcripts come from, who needs to see follow-ups, and how urgent items should be flagged. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to name where transcripts come from before you build around a guess, and the scope document becomes the brief for every run after it.

items: Where memos get recorded and transcribed.
Where extracted items should land so they don't pile into one list.
Whether follow-up drafts always wait for review or only above a stakes threshold.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common connectors are a notes or task app ([Notion](#tooltip-notion), Apple Notes, Todoist), a calendar (Google Calendar), and messaging to send follow-ups (Gmail, [Slack](#tooltip-slack), iMessage). The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on a real transcript. The prompt below is an example of the core task. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Turn a raw voice-memo transcript into decisions, action items, and drafted follow-ups.

Context: [Paste your transcript.] I record after [calls / meetings / planning walks]. Action items usually involve [names or roles].

Rules:
- Separate decisions, action items, and open questions.
- Give each action item an owner and deadline, or mark it "not specified."
- Draft one follow-up message per action item; never send it.
- Ignore filler and hedging; extract only firm statements.
- Output as three sections: Decisions, Action Items as a table, Follow-up Drafts.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming decisions, action items, and open questions as separate categories keeps a passing comment from getting logged as a commitment.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Owners and deadlines present, follow-ups drafted and not sent, filler left out?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what got missed or overstated, and fold the correction into the rules.

items: File items straight into the right project by connecting your notes app through a [tool connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors).
Build a weekly digest of everything extracted across memos.
Flag open questions that keep recurring across recordings.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat turn the scope bar into pass/fail checks and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each action item list, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, memos processed, items extracted, items missed or misread, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make recurring misses visible after a week of entries.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a week straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults instead of a blank chat. When the log shows the same check failing again and again, that gap is a candidate for a skill of its own. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. A rambling transcript produces vague items unless you tell the tool to ignore hedging, so give it that [context](#tooltip-context) every run. A passing comment can also read as firmer than it was, which is why every follow-up draft waits on you to send.
